title: Comedonal Lupus: Case Series and Literature Review.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Comedonal lupus (CL) is a rare variant of cutaneous lupus erythematosus.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to describe the clinical, dermoscopic, and histopathological characteristics of CL.
METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of patients diagnosed with CL in our dermatology department between January 2020 and August 2025, complemented by a literature review.
RESULTS: Seven patients were identified (sex ratio 0.4; mean age 48.2 years). Lesions predominantly affected the face, scalp, and ears. Four patients exhibited acneiform lesions combining comedones and milialike pseudocysts, and two showed worm-eaten scars. The perioral region, cheeks, nose, and eyebrows were the most frequently involved facial sites. Three patients presented with sharply demarcated alopecic scalp plaques with a dirty-brown appearance and central comedones. Facial dermoscopy consistently demonstrated arborizing vessels, comedones, opalescent yellow structures, follicular keratotic plugs, rosettes, a blue-white veil, peripheral pigmentation, and, while trichoscopy revealed central whitishred areas, loss of follicular openings, yellow keratotic plugs, irregular pigmentation, and comedones. Histopathology of skin and scalp lesions showed epidermal atrophy, orthokeratosis, basal vacuolar degeneration, basement membrane thickening, dilated follicular ostia with keratin plugs, and perivascular and perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrates. Direct immunofluorescence demonstrated granular C3 deposition along the basement membrane in four cases. ANA was positive in five patients, and anti-dsDNA antibodies were detected in the single systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) case. Treatment with topical corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine achieved partial improvement and stabilization in most cases, while the SLE patient showed marked improvement with systemic therapy and photoprotection.
CONCLUSIONS: CL often mimics acne, which may delay diagnosis; dermoscopy assists recognition, yet treatment outcomes remain suboptimal.

title: A Rare Case of Fulminant Guillain-Barre Syndrome as the Cardinal Presenting Feature of New Onset Pediatric Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Here we present a complex case of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presenting initially as fulminant Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). This particular manifestation of neuropsychiatric lupus is uncommon but can be severe and even life threatening. Increasing providers' awareness of the overlap between lupus and GBS will improve diagnostic accuracy and timing as well as expedite appropriate therapies, which may differ from typical GBS treatment.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 12-year-old previously healthy Hispanic female presented with subacute onset vision changes and imbalance with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and hyporeflexia. Given her classic clinical triad and suspicion for GBS variant Miller Fischer syndrome (MFS), neuroaxis imaging was obtained. MRI showed cranial nerve and ventral nerve root enhancement, and cytoalbuminologic dissociation seen on cerebrospinal fluid analysis also supported this diagnosis. Weakness including the facial and bulbar muscles and the extremities progressed rapidly and threatened respiratory functions, so the patient was intubated. Typical treatments for GBS including intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and plasma exchange (PLEX) were insufficient to manage symptoms, and additional evaluations supported a diagnosis of SLE with nephritis. Coordinated care between neuroimmunology and rheumatology enabled rapid escalation of therapy to include high-dose intravenous steroid pulses, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab. Together, these therapies eventually stabilized the patient, and with support from neuropsychology, psychiatry, and rehabilitation medicine, she was able to discharge from the hospital after 115 days of admission. She has remained in remission on maintenance immunosuppression including mycophenolate mofetil as well as hydroxychloroquine.
CONCLUSIONS: Neuropsychiatric lupus can be difficult to diagnose and manage, but its severity necessitates vigilance and aggressive management. In the current case, the isolated neurological symptoms at presentation consistent with GBS could have delayed diagnosis, but neuroimmunology and rheumatology were consulted early, and appropriate diagnostic testing was performed. The patient's multidisciplinary team worked closely together to appropriately escalate her treatment beyond what is typical for GBS, ultimately leading to remission of her neuropsychiatric symptoms and recovery of her baseline neurological status. This case highlights the complex nature of neuropsychiatric lupus, suggests that SLE should be on the differential in atypical or difficult-to-treat cases of GBS, and underscores the need for coordinated interdisciplinary care to achieve best outcomes for these patients.

title: Autoimmune Overlap of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Myasthenia Gravis: A Case Report and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies.
abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and myasthenia gravis (MG) are autoimmune disorders that predominantly affect women and may coexist, though their overlap remains rare. Shared mechanisms, including loss of immune tolerance, B-cell hyperactivity, and dysregulated cytokine signaling, are thought to underlie this association. We report the case of a 56-year-old woman diagnosed with seronegative MG after presenting with progressive proximal weakness, ocular involvement, and electrophysiologic evidence of neuromuscular junction dysfunction. She was stabilized on IVIG, pyridostigmine, and azathioprine. Four years later, she developed a malar rash, polyarthralgia, and bilateral upper-extremity numbness; serologic evaluation confirmed SLE and revealed newly detectable acetylcholine receptor binding antibodies, representing her first positive MG serologic marker. Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) and methotrexate were added to her regimen. Efgartigimod alfa, a neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) antagonist, was subsequently initiated for persistent MG and produced marked improvement in MG Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) scores. Her SLE-related joint symptoms also improved, although SLE-directed therapy had been adjusted during the same period. However, cyclic dosing resulted in consistent symptomatic wear-off in the days preceding each treatment cycle. Transition to nipocalimab, a fixed-schedule anti-FcRn monoclonal antibody providing continuous IgG suppression, is under multidisciplinary consideration. This case highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic complexity of SLE-MG overlap and suggests that FcRn inhibition may offer a mechanistically rational approach to IgG-mediated disease in both conditions, a possibility that warrants further study.

title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus-Associated Autoimmune Myelofibrosis Mimicking TAFRO Syndrome: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multisystem autoimmune disorder with diverse hematologic manifestations, rarely complicated by autoimmune myelofibrosis (AIMF), a non-clonal and potentially reversible form of marrow fibrosis. Differentiating SLE-associated AIMF from TAFRO syndrome can be difficult because both conditions share overlapping features, including cytopenias, effusions, renal dysfunction, systemic inflammation, and reticulin fibrosis. We describe a 33-year-old woman who presented with recurrent low-grade fever, pedal edema, ascites, and dyspnea. Laboratory evaluation revealed pancytopenia, Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia, proteinuric renal disease, elevated inflammatory markers, antinuclear antibodies (ANA) positivity (1:2560, speckled pattern), high anti-dsDNA titers, and low complement C3 levels. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated grade III reticulin fibrosis with increased megakaryocytes without significant atypia, while testing for myeloproliferative driver mutations, including JAK2, CALR, and MPL, was negative. Although the patient fulfilled several clinical criteria suggestive of TAFRO syndrome, lymph node biopsy showed only reactive hyperplasia without features of idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease, supporting a diagnosis of SLE-associated AIMF. She was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral prednisolone, hydroxychloroquine, intravenous immunoglobulin, and rituximab, resulting in marked clinical and hematologic improvement, with remission achieved within six weeks. This case highlights the importance of careful serologic, histopathologic, and clinicopathologic correlation in distinguishing AIMF from TAFRO-like syndromes, as prompt recognition and immunosuppressive therapy can lead to reversal of marrow fibrosis and favorable outcomes.
